summary: Specifies the steps a host takes to configure its own IPv6 addresses automatically on an interface. It lets a host form addresses without a server handing them out. It was a draft standard, replaced by RFC 4862.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC explains how a computer with IPv6 gives itself an address. The computer makes up a number that identifies its network card, puts it after a standard prefix, and then asks the network whether anyone else is using that address. Routers on the network announce which address ranges are in use, so the computer can build further addresses without asking a server for them.

subtitle: How an IPv6 host builds its own address and checks that nobody else has taken it.

tldr.problem: Plugging a machine into an IPv6 network should not require an administrator to write down an address for it, and the address a machine invents for itself must not clash with one another machine has already taken.
tldr.mechanism: The host builds a link-local address from the well-known link-local prefix and an interface identifier it can supply itself, then checks it is free by asking the link. Routers advertise the prefixes in use, and the host combines a prefix with the same interface identifier to make further addresses.
tldr.outcome: A small network needs no address server at all, and a large one needs no address server for its addresses, though it can still use one for other settings. The document was a Draft Standard and has been replaced by RFC 4862.

facts.label: Default DupAddrDetectTransmits
facts.value: 1, a single transmission with no retransmissions

facts.label: Router Advertisement flags
facts.value: M for managed address configuration, O for other stateful configuration

today: RFC 2462 was published in December 1998 as a Draft Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 4862, which restates IPv6 stateless address autoconfiguration. It had itself obsoleted RFC 1971.

sections.title: What Autoconfiguration Covers
sections.content:
The RFC specifies the steps a host takes in deciding how to autoconfigure its interfaces: creating a link-local address and verifying its uniqueness on the link, deciding what information should be configured, and deciding whether addresses should come from the stateless mechanism, the stateful mechanism or both. It defines the process for generating a link-local address, the process for generating site-local and global addresses statelessly, and the Duplicate Address Detection procedure. The details of stateful autoconfiguration are specified elsewhere.

The two mechanisms are alternatives that complement each other. Stateless autoconfiguration needs no manual configuration of hosts, minimal configuration of routers and no additional servers: a host generates its own addresses from a combination of information available locally and information advertised by routers. Routers advertise the prefixes that identify the subnets on a link, and the host generates an interface identifier that is unique for that interface; the address is the two joined together. In the stateful model, hosts obtain addresses and configuration from a server that keeps a database of which address belongs to which host. A site uses the stateless approach when it does not care exactly which addresses its hosts get, as long as they are unique and routable, and the stateful approach when it wants tight control. Both may run at the same time, and the administrator chooses by setting fields in Router Advertisement messages.

Addresses are leased to an interface for a fixed, possibly infinite, time. An address first becomes preferred, meaning its use in arbitrary communication is unrestricted, and later becomes deprecated in anticipation that the binding will end; while deprecated, its use is discouraged but not forbidden. A node runs Duplicate Address Detection on all addresses before assigning them to an interface, whether they came from the stateless mechanism, the stateful mechanism or manual configuration.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 has two ways for a computer to get an address. The stateless way is for the computer to work it out itself from what the routers say; the stateful way is to ask a server that keeps a list. This RFC covers the stateless way, and the check that stops two computers from choosing the same address.

sections.title: Why a Host Should Configure Itself
sections.content:
The RFC states five goals for the design. Manual configuration of individual machines before connecting them to the network should not be required, so a mechanism is needed that lets a host obtain or create unique addresses for each of its interfaces. Each interface is assumed to be able to provide a unique identifier for itself, and in the simplest case that identifier is the interface's link-layer address; the identifier can then be combined with a prefix to form an address.

A small site of machines attached to a single link should not need a stateful server or a router as a prerequisite for communicating. Plug-and-play communication is achieved with link-local addresses, which have a well-known prefix identifying the shared link, and a host forms one by appending its interface identifier to that prefix. A large site with several networks and routers should not need a stateful address configuration server either: routers generate periodic Router Advertisements that carry options listing the set of active prefixes on a link, and hosts use those prefixes to build site-local and global addresses.

Address configuration should make it possible to renumber a site gracefully. Renumbering works through leasing addresses to interfaces and assigning several addresses to the same interface: the lease lifetimes give a site the mechanism for phasing out old prefixes, and the second address gives a transition period during which both the new address and the one being retired work at the same time. Finally, administrators need to be able to say whether stateless autoconfiguration, stateful autoconfiguration or both should be used, and Router Advertisements carry flags that specify this.
sections.plainLanguage: The design goals are practical: no administrator should have to type addresses into machines, a small network should work with no server at all, a big network should not need a server just for addresses, and changing the addresses a site uses should not break the connections running on them.

sections.title: What Happens When an Interface Comes Up
sections.content:
Autoconfiguration is performed on multicast-capable links and begins when such an interface is enabled, for example during system startup. Nodes begin by generating a link-local address for the interface, formed by appending the interface identifier to the well-known link-local prefix. Before that address can be used, the node must try to verify that it is not already in use: it sends a Neighbor Solicitation with the tentative address as the target, and a node already using the address answers with a Neighbor Advertisement, while a node trying the same address at the same time sends a solicitation of its own. How many solicitations are sent and how long to wait between them is link-specific and may be set by system management.

If the tentative link-local address turns out not to be unique, autoconfiguration stops and the interface needs manual configuration. To make recovery simpler, an administrator should be able to supply an alternate interface identifier that overrides the default one, so that the mechanism can be applied again with the new identifier.

Once the address is known to be unique it is assigned to the interface, and the node has IP-level connectivity with its neighbours. The next phase is obtaining a Router Advertisement or deciding that no routers are present; if none are, the host should fall back on stateful autoconfiguration. Routers advertise periodically, which is often longer than a configuring host wants to wait, so the host sends Router Solicitations to the all-routers multicast group to get an advertisement quickly. Advertisements carry two flags: a managed address configuration flag saying whether hosts should use stateful autoconfiguration for addresses, and an other stateful configuration flag saying whether they should use it for information other than addresses. They also carry zero or more Prefix Information options, each giving a subnet prefix together with the lifetimes for addresses made from it. Because routers advertise periodically, the host keeps receiving new advertisements and adds to and refreshes what it learned earlier.

All addresses must be tested for uniqueness before assignment, but for stateless addresses the uniqueness comes entirely from the interface identifier. So once a link-local address has been checked, further addresses built from the same identifier need not be tested one by one, while addresses obtained manually or through the stateful mechanism should each be tested individually. A host may generate its link-local address and check it at the same time as it waits for a Router Advertisement, because a router can take several seconds to answer a solicitation and doing the two steps one after another makes autoconfiguration much slower.
sections.plainLanguage: When a network card is switched on, the computer makes up a link-local address, asks the network whether it is free, and starts using it. It then asks the routers which address ranges are in use and builds further addresses from those. The two steps can run at the same time, because waiting for the routers is the slow part.

sections.title: Forming and Verifying the Link-Local Address
sections.content:
A node forms a link-local address whenever an interface becomes enabled, which happens at system startup, after a temporary interface failure, when the interface attaches to a link for the first time, or when system management re-enables it. The address is formed by prepending the well-known link-local prefix FE80::0 of the appropriate length to the interface identifier: if the identifier is N bits long, it replaces the rightmost N zero bits of the prefix. If the identifier is more than 118 bits long, autoconfiguration fails and manual configuration is required. Interface identifiers will typically be 64 bits long and based on EUI-64 identifiers. A link-local address has an infinite preferred and valid lifetime; it is never timed out.

Duplicate Address Detection is performed on unicast addresses before they are assigned to an interface whose DupAddrDetectTransmits variable is greater than zero, and it must take place on all unicast addresses whether they came from stateful, stateless or manual configuration, with two exceptions: it must not be performed on anycast addresses, and for a set of addresses formed from the same interface identifier it is enough to test the link-local address generated from that identifier, after which an implementation may skip the rest. An address on which the procedure is being applied is tentative: the interface accepts Neighbor Discovery packets about it but silently discards other packets sent to it.

Before sending a Neighbor Solicitation the interface joins the all-nodes multicast address and the solicited-node multicast address of the tentative address. The first means the node receives advertisements from nodes already using the address; the second means two nodes trying the same address at the same time detect each other. The node sends DupAddrDetectTransmits solicitations separated by RetransTimer milliseconds, with the target address set to the address being checked, the source set to the unspecified address and the destination set to the solicited-node multicast address of the target. If the solicitation is the first message sent after the interface is initialised, the node should delay it by a random delay of up to MAX_RTR_SOLICITATION_DELAY, which relieves congestion when many machines start at once and helps avoid races; while delaying, the interface must still receive and process datagrams sent to the all-nodes or solicited-node multicast address.

On receiving a valid solicitation, behaviour depends on the target. If the target is not tentative, the message is processed as in Neighbor Discovery. If the target is tentative and the source address is a unicast address, the sender is resolving that address and the solicitation is ignored. A node must not respond to a solicitation for a tentative address of its own. A solicitation whose source is the unspecified address comes from a node running the same check: if it came from another node, the address is a duplicate and neither node may use it; if it came from the node itself, because the interface loops multicast packets back, it shows nothing. Two conditions mean the tentative address is not unique: a solicitation for it arrives before the node has sent one, which happens when two nodes start the check at different moments; or more solicitations arrive than the loopback behaviour would explain, which happens when two nodes start at roughly the same moment. A valid Neighbor Advertisement for the tentative address also means it is not unique.

When the check fails, the address must not be assigned and the node should log an error, and if the address is a link-local one formed from an interface identifier, the interface should be disabled. The RFC notes that the method is not completely reliable: duplicates can still arise, for example if the link was partitioned while the check was running.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is made by putting the machine's own card number after the standard link-local prefix. The computer then asks the network whether anyone else is using it: it sends a request from the null address to a group address derived from the address being tested. If another machine answers, or if another machine is testing the same address at the same time, the address is dropped and the interface is disabled.

sections.title: Global and Site-Local Addresses and Their Lifetimes
sections.content:
Global and site-local addresses are formed by appending an interface identifier to a prefix of the appropriate length, and the prefixes come from Prefix Information options in Router Advertisements. On receipt of a valid advertisement the host copies the M bit into its ManagedFlag and the O bit into its OtherConfigFlag. When ManagedFlag changes from false to true the host should start the stateful address autoconfiguration protocol, requesting both address and other information; when the flag changes from true to false the host should keep running it. The O flag is processed the same way for information other than addresses. A host must not restart the stateful protocol if it is already taking part in it because of an earlier advertisement.

For each Prefix Information option the host checks several conditions. If the autonomous flag is not set, the option is ignored. If the prefix is the link-local prefix, the option is ignored. If the preferred lifetime is greater than the valid lifetime, the option is ignored. If the advertised prefix does not match the prefix of an address already held and the valid lifetime is not zero, an address is formed by combining the advertised prefix with the link's interface identifier, and the sum of the prefix length and the identifier length must equal 128 bits or the option must be ignored; the new address is added to the interface's list with its preferred and valid lifetimes taken from the option.

When the advertised prefix matches one already held, the lifetime handling depends on what was received and what was stored. If the received lifetime is greater than two hours or greater than the stored lifetime, the stored lifetime is updated. If the stored lifetime is at most two hours and the received lifetime is no larger than the stored one, the prefix is ignored, unless the advertisement it came from was authenticated, in which case the stored lifetime should be set to the received value. Otherwise the stored lifetime is reset to two hours. The RFC gives the reason: these rules answer a denial of service attack in which a bogus advertisement carries prefixes with very small valid lifetimes, which without the rules could make all of a node's addresses expire at once. Legitimate advertisements, which come periodically, cancel such short lifetimes before they take effect.

When an address's preferred lifetime expires it becomes deprecated. It should still be used as a source address in existing communications but not in new ones if an alternative is available with sufficient scope, and IP and the layers above must keep accepting datagrams sent to it. When the valid lifetime expires, the address becomes invalid: it must not be used as a source address and must not be recognised as a destination on a receiving interface. Renumbering works through these two states, since upper layers such as TCP cannot change the address of an open connection, so the deprecation period has to be long enough that most connections have moved to the new address before the old one stops working.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the routers say which address ranges are in use, the computer joins its own card number to each of them. Every address carries two clocks: one says when it should stop being used for new connections, and the other says when it must not be used at all. The gap between the two is what lets a site change its addresses without breaking running connections.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Stateless address autoconfiguration lets a host join a network, configure an address and start communicating without ever registering or authenticating itself with the local site. The RFC notes that although this allows unauthorised users to connect to and use a network, the threat is inherent in the Internet architecture: any node with a physical attachment to a network can generate an address using a variety of ad hoc techniques that gives it connectivity.

The use of Duplicate Address Detection opens the door to a denial of service attack. Any node can answer a Neighbor Solicitation for a tentative address, which makes the node asking reject that address as a duplicate. The RFC describes this as similar to other attacks that involve spoofing Neighbor Discovery messages, and says it can be addressed by requiring that Neighbor Discovery packets be authenticated.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone with a cable can join the network, because nothing asks them to register first; the RFC accepts that as part of how the Internet is built. The check that an address is free can also be abused: a node that answers every address check can stop other machines from configuring themselves.

viz.caption: THE MESSAGES OF AN AUTOCONFIGURING HOST (ILLUSTRATIVE, NOT FROM THE RFC)

messages.label: Neighbor Solicitation
messages.note: Sent from the unspecified address to the solicited-node multicast address, asking whether the tentative address is already taken.

messages.label: Neighbor Advertisement
messages.note: Only sent if the address is already in use, in which case the host discards it.

messages.label: Router Solicitation
messages.note: Sent to the all-routers multicast group to get a Router Advertisement without waiting for the next periodic one.

messages.label: Router Advertisement
messages.note: Carries the M and O flags and the Prefix Information options that give the prefixes in use on the link.

viz.caption: AN ADDRESS BUILT FROM A PREFIX AND AN INTERFACE IDENTIFIER

fields.name: Link prefix
fields.desc: FE80::0 for a link-local address, or a prefix from a Prefix Information option.

fields.name: Interface identifier
fields.desc: The identifier the interface supplies, typically 64 bits based on EUI-64. Prefix and identifier together must total 128 bits.

viz.caption: THE FOUR STATES OF AN AUTOCONFIGURED ADDRESS

cells: Its use in arbitrary communication is unrestricted.
As a source or destination address.
The binding to the interface is about to end.
Still valid, but new connections should use a preferred address.
The valid lifetime has expired and the address may be reused elsewhere.
Must not be used as a source or as a destination.
Its uniqueness on the link is still being checked.
Only Neighbor Discovery packets about it are accepted; the rest are discarded.
